lab_title: The Double Helix and Semiconservative DNA Replication
top_level_objectives: Identify the structural components of the DNA double helix, including the antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones and inward-projecting nitrogenous bases
Apply the complementary base-pairing rules (A-T with two hydrogen bonds, G-C with three) to predict strand sequences
Explain how the 5'-to-3' directionality and antiparallel orientation of the backbone constrain replication
Describe the roles of helicase, single-strand binding proteins, DNA polymerase, and DNA ligase at the replication fork
Explain why replication is semiconservative and why it produces continuous leading-strand and discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis

scenes.brief_purpose: Orient students to the overall three-dimensional form of DNA and establish the vocabulary used throughout the lab.
key_visuals: A slowly rotating full-length DNA double helix floating at eye level
The two sugar-phosphate backbones highlighted as ribbons spiraling around a common central axis
A faint vertical axis line running through the center of the helix
student_actions: Rotate and orbit the helix to view it from multiple angles
Tap the two backbones to hear how they coil around the shared axis
Confirm they can distinguish the outer backbones from the inner region before continuing

scenes.brief_purpose: Break the helix into its molecular components so students can identify backbones, bases, and the rungs formed by paired bases.
key_visuals: An unwound, ladder-like segment of DNA showing alternating sugar and phosphate units along each backbone
Color-coded nitrogenous bases (A, T, G, C) projecting inward from each backbone
Dashed hydrogen bonds bridging the paired bases across the ladder
student_actions: Tap individual sugar and phosphate groups to label the backbone repeating unit
Select each base to reveal its name and single-letter code
Trace a base pair across the ladder to see the hydrogen bonds connecting the two strands

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students discover and apply complementary base pairing, including the different number of hydrogen bonds for A-T versus G-C.
key_visuals: A partially built helix with several bases on one strand exposed and unpaired
A palette of loose A, T, G, and C bases the student can drag into place
Animated hydrogen bonds that form (two for A-T, three for G-C) when a correct pair is made and reject incorrect pairings
student_actions: Drag complementary bases onto the exposed template strand to complete each pair
Observe two versus three hydrogen bonds forming for A-T and G-C respectively
Predict the full sequence of the complementary strand given the template sequence

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish that the two strands run in opposite 5'-to-3' directions and connect this directionality to backbone chemistry.
key_visuals: The double helix with 5' and 3' end labels highlighted on both strands
Directional arrows running along each backbone pointing in opposite directions
A zoomed inset showing the phosphate (5') and hydroxyl (3') ends of the sugar-phosphate backbone
student_actions: Label the 5' and 3' end of each strand using draggable tags
Follow the directional arrows to confirm the strands are antiparallel
Answer a checkpoint question about why one strand runs 3' to 5' when its partner runs 5' to 3'

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the enzymes that open and stabilize the helix at the start of replication.
key_visuals: A helicase molecule wedging into the helix and splitting it into a Y-shaped replication fork
Single-strand binding proteins coating the separated parental strands to keep them apart
The two exposed template strands with their bases now available for pairing
student_actions: Position helicase at the fork and watch it unwind the double helix
Attach single-strand binding proteins to the exposed strands to stabilize them
Identify which portion of the molecule is now single-stranded template

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how DNA polymerase's 5'-to-3'-only synthesis, combined with antiparallel templates, forces continuous versus discontinuous synthesis.
key_visuals: DNA polymerase adding nucleotides continuously along the leading strand toward the moving fork
DNA polymerase synthesizing the lagging strand in short Okazaki fragments pointing away from the fork
DNA ligase sealing the gaps between adjacent Okazaki fragments
student_actions: Guide DNA polymerase along both templates and note it can only extend in the 5'-to-3' direction
Assemble the lagging strand as a series of Okazaki fragments
Use DNA ligase to join the fragments and compare the smooth leading strand with the patched lagging strand

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the whole process by showing that each daughter molecule retains one parental strand and one new strand.
key_visuals: Two completed daughter double helices side by side
Original parental strands shown in one color and newly synthesized strands in another within each daughter molecule
A summary diagram tracing one parental strand into each of the two products
student_actions: Color-code parental versus newly synthesized strands in each daughter molecule
Confirm that every daughter helix contains exactly one old and one new strand
Complete a final summary quiz linking antiparallel structure, base pairing, and semiconservative replication
